name: Congo Swahili
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.source_named: Ferrari, Aurelia, Marcel Kalunga & Georges Mulumbwa. 2014. Le swahili de Lubumbashi: grammaire, textes, lexique. Paris: Karthala. (Also Kapanga 1991 diss. on Shaba Swahili.) Not openly online.
earlier_scan.note: Full grammar of the Lubumbashi (Shaba/Congo Swahili) variety exists in print; accent section not readable online.

new_statements.quote: L'accent, en swahili de Lubumbashi, porte souvent sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du groupe rythmique, comme en swahili standard. Elle apparaît cependant parfois dans certains emprunts au français sur la dernière syllabe du groupe rythmique. L'accentuation peut être double, notamment pour les conjugaisons au futur négatif où elle apparaît sur la première et sur l'avant-dernière syllabes de la forme verbale. Cette double accentuation permet de distinguer l'affirmatif du négatif. [...] Il existe d'autres exemples où l'accentuation peut varier et avoir un caractère distinctif. Kya 'mwisho avec un accent sur la pénultième signifie « la dernière chose » alors que kya mwi'sho avec un accent sur la dernière syllabe signifie « le dernier d'une course ».
new_statements.translation: In Lubumbashi Swahili the accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the rhythmic group, as in Standard Swahili. It does, however, sometimes appear on the last syllable of the rhythmic group in certain loans from French. Accentuation can be double, notably in the negative future, where it appears on the first and on the penultimate syllables of the verb form; this double accentuation distinguishes the affirmative from the negative. [...] There are other examples where the accentuation can vary and be distinctive: kya 'mwisho with penultimate accent means 'the last thing' whereas kya mwi'sho with final accent means 'the last one in a race'.
new_statements.citation: Ferrari, Aurélia, Marcel Kalunga & Georges Mulumbwa. 2014. Le swahili de Lubumbashi: grammaire, textes, lexique. Paris: Karthala.
new_statements.locator: §1.1.4 'L'accentuation', pp. 17-18 (also p. 19 and 'Les tons et l'accentuation en SL', p. 22; p. 66)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word/rhythmic-group accent is on the penultimate syllable, as in Standard Swahili; deviations: final accent in some French loanwords and in words where an identical VV sequence has been reduced (tamaa > ta'ma, jogoo > jo'go, juu > 'dju, p.19 after Kapanga 1993); an additional accent on the first syllable (the subject prefix) in negative-future forms ('ata'kuya 'he will not come' vs ata'kuya 'he will come'; p.18, p.66); a handful of lexicalised contrasts (kya 'mwisho vs kya mwi'sho). Some limited tone appears under contact with surrounding tone languages (àkà habitual vs áká remote), though the variety derives from non-tonal Swahili (p.22). Kapanga 1993:443 independently states that in both Shaba Swahili and East African Swahili 'the tonal accent normally falls on the penultimate syllables', with final accent in tamá, jogó, mzé, jú after vowel reduction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary-stress rule given; the only multi-accent case described is the 'double accentuation' (first syllable + penult) of negative-future verb forms (p.18, p.66).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in some French loans; final accent after reduction of identical vowel sequences (ta'ma, jo'go, 'dju; Kapanga 1993 adds mzé); double accent (initial + penult) in negative future; lexical contrast kya 'mwisho vs kya mwi'sho; the lexicon marks any non-penultimate accent with '. Limited contact-induced tonal distinctions (àkà vs áká).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the 'groupe rythmique' (rhythmic/phonological group), explicitly equated with the Standard Swahili pattern; examples are citation-form words and inflected verb forms. Kapanga 1993 calls it 'tonal accent' on the penultimate syllable of the word.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Lubumbashi (Katanga/Shaba) urban variety of Congo Swahili ('swahili de Lubumbashi', 'Shaba Swahili'), one of several regional varieties subsumed under cong1236 [swc] (others: Kivu/Bukavu-Goma Swahili, Kisangani Swahili, Ituri Kingwana/Bunia Swahili, Lualaba Kingwana). Glottolog lists Ferrari et al. 2014, Kapanga 1991 and de Rooij 1995 under cong1236 itself; no separate glottocode for the Lubumbashi variety is known to me. Harris & Lukoff 1942 'Kingwana-Swahili' is based on one speaker from Lisala whose forms look like Bangala/Lingala and should not be taken as representative of Congo Swahili.

sources.citation: Harris, Zellig S. & Fred Lukoff. 1942. The phonemes of Kingwana-Swahili. Journal of the American Oriental Society 62(4): 333-338.
sources.note: §1.33: three phonetic degrees of stress; §2.11: tone and stress pattern jointly by word — in disyllables either first vowel high tone + loud stress and second low/zero, or first low + final not low/zero; in trisyllables the high/loud vowel is the penult in pattern 1; marked with an accent on the penult vs on the final. CAVEAT: the single informant is from Lisala (Bangala area) and the cited forms (libanga 'stone', nabwaki 'I threw', bango 'they', mai 'water', motema-type nouns) look like Bangala/Lingala rather than Swahili, so this is not a reliable description of Congo Swahili prosody.

sources.note: p.443: 'in both ShS and EAS, the tonal accent normally falls on the penultimate syllables; however, in (5) [tamaa > tamá, jogoo > jogó, mzee > mzé, juu > jú] tone falls on the last syllable' — i.e. penultimate accent with final accent arising from identical-vowel reduction.
